facts.value: Two weeks after respiratory infection symptoms, dyspnea progressed to NYHA III with leg edema and abdominal pain; no chest pain or dizziness initially.
Peripheral edema and bradycardia, heart rate 42/min.
No P waves; narrow-QRS escape rhythm at 42/min.

provider_metadata.assistant_note: The ECG shows no P waves and a narrow-QRS escape rhythm at 42/min. He also has post-viral progressive heart failure. The main possibilities are acute myocarditis with atrial standstill or conduction disease, and hyperkalaemia or another metabolic cause. I'm ordering stat labs to check potassium and electrolytes (chemistry), myocardial injury (troponin), heart failure severity (NT-proBNP) and inflammation.

facts.value: TTE: preserved LV systolic function; dilated LA and RV; impaired RV function; severe tricuspid regurgitation; estimated systolic PA pressure 58 mm Hg; only mild mitral regurgitation.

args.summary: 35M with progressive exertional dyspnea (NYHA III), leg edema and abdominal pain 2 weeks after a respiratory infection (hpi_001). HR 42/min with peripheral edema (physical_exam_004). ECG: absent P waves, narrow-QRS escape rhythm at 42/min (ecg_005), suggesting atrial standstill/junctional escape. hs-TnT 31 ng/L, NT-proBNP 432 pg/mL (lab_006, lab_007). TTE: preserved LVEF, dilated LA/RV, impaired RV function, severe TR, sPAP 58 mm Hg (ecg_009). CTPA: no PE; RV dilatation, bilateral pleural effusions, hepatic vein reflux (imaging_010). CMR: LA late gadolinium enhancement with borderline edema, no ventricular scar (imaging_014). Picture suggests post-viral atrial myocarditis causing atrial standstill with bradycardia-related right heart failure and congestive hepatopathy.
working_diagnoses: Post-viral (atrial) myocarditis with acquired atrial standstill and junctional escape bradycardia
Right heart failure with severe functional TR and congestive hepatopathy/effusions
Cardiac sarcoidosis or other infiltrative atrial cardiomyopathy
Genetic atrial cardiomyopathy (e.g., SCN5A/NPPA-related atrial standstill)
Hyperkalemia/metabolic or drug-induced sinoatrial arrest (to exclude)
next_actions: Check electrolytes (K+), renal and liver function, TSH and medication history to exclude reversible causes
Continuous telemetry with transcutaneous pacing available; temporary pacing if unstable
Cautious IV loop diuretic for congestion
EP assessment for permanent pacemaker (VVI, since atrial capture is unlikely in atrial standstill) plus anticoagulation for thromboembolic risk

args.rationale: Symptomatic bradycardia at 42/min. The ECG shows no P waves and a narrow-QRS escape rhythm, consistent with acquired atrial standstill (ecg_005). The patient has NYHA III right heart failure: severe TR, impaired RV function, systolic PA pressure 58 mm Hg, bilateral pleural effusions and contrast reflux into the hepatic veins (ecg_009, imaging_010). Troponin is raised (lab_007). Cardiac MRI shows left atrial LGE with borderline edema, suggesting atrial myocarditis (imaging_014). The escape rhythm may fail, so he needs continuous monitoring with pacing immediately available until a permanent device is implanted. Electrolytes, renal, thyroid and liver results were not available in the source. Reversible causes are therefore not yet excluded.
args.followup_or_handoff: Hand off to CCU/cardiology and electrophysiology. Keep continuous telemetry with transcutaneous pacing pads on. Place a temporary transvenous wire if he becomes unstable. Urgent EP study and permanent pacemaker (VVI(R) or conduction-system pacing) as ordered. Continue IV furosemide 40 mg twice daily with daily weight, fluid balance, creatinine and potassium. Urgently check electrolytes (especially K+), renal and liver function, and TSH. Avoid AV-nodal blocking drugs. Consider anticoagulation for thromboembolic risk from atrial standstill after bleeding risk is assessed, given ulcerative colitis. Review mesalazine as a possible cause of hypersensitivity myocarditis together with gastroenterology. Assess for sarcoidosis and consider genetic testing (SCN5A/NPPA). Repeat cardiac MRI and echo, then follow up in the cardiology and device clinic.
